item.title: Staff Post - Wikiwalk Proposal
item.content:encoded:
Timer Expired. Edits made as discussed below. Author may revert at any time.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

Alright, so there are a few potential links for me to suggest here. First off, if the main goal of containment is blocking the transmission of the satellite, that seems something right up MTF Mu-4's alley, and a quick nod can be sent there way in the containment procs, linking to their MTF page. Additionally, I would imagine the SCP Foundation is likely considering it a possibility this signal might be interacting with SCP-2399 in some way. As such, I am recommending the following edits:

Changing this:

Methods of containing SCP-471 are currently being investigated. Primary goal of containment is to block the non-terrestrial transmissions emanating from it, with a secondary goal of acquiring and studying SCP-471 itself.

To this:

Methods of containing SCP-471 are currently being investigated. Primary goal of containment is to block the non-terrestrial transmissions emanating from it, with a secondary goal of acquiring and studying SCP-471 itself. MTF Mu-4 ("Debuggers") is currently tasked with blocking SCP-471's transmissions.

Changing this:

While attempting to glean the purpose of the integer values identified by BOMB-2, the Foundation discovered a copy of the signal transmitted by SCP-471, much weaker and with an 88 minute delay, being transmitted back at Earth. Investigation revealed that SCP-471 was transmitting its signal in such a way that it was amplified by the magnetosphere of Jupiter and broadcast in all directions. The copied signal evaded detection because it blended in with the background static naturally produced by Jupiter.

To this:

While attempting to glean the purpose of the integer values identified by BOMB-2, the Foundation discovered a copy of the signal transmitted by SCP-471, much weaker and with an 88 minute delay, being transmitted back at Earth. Investigation revealed that SCP-471 was transmitting its signal in such a way that it was amplified by the magnetosphere of Jupiter and broadcast in all directions. The copied signal evaded detection because it blended in with the background static naturally produced by Jupiter. Investigation into the possible interaction of this signal with SCP-2399 and other Jovian based anomalies is ongoing.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.title: Well now
item.content:encoded:
I've been directed to this by Project Heimdall and it's a bit…off.

First of all: All the evidence indicates this is a probe able to mimic a human weather satellite effectively. It's potentially gathering intelligence for an invasion attempt, creating an unblockable data signal which destroys any unauthorised computer trying to make sense of it, and can deploy terrifying technology against the most EMP-shielded probes the Foundation can build into the bargain when they are sent to look at it. Surely its hostility qualifies it as Keter?

Next: The Foundation basically has a choice: jam it/destroy it or let it carry on looking at us. The implication is that the Foundation would rather leave it in place (possibly to avoid appearing to declare war on the SCP's creators?) but can destroy it. I see the preference for keeping it intact rather than destroying it but I'm not convinced-I would have thought that creating a stealth probe that mimics a human satellite is beyond the 'we come in peace' stage. I like it as uncontained while the foundation works out what to do (I'm working on a draft SCP along those lines myself) but a memo about them contemplating its destruction would be nice.

Next: it knows we know about it. What if we attempt direct communication with it? (I wouldn't want it to respond; it's more menacing voiceless.)

Finally: The data that destroys computers. Oookay, I see that. It's anomalously encrypted and maybe the probe's electronics can sense a computer thinking about it from orbit. But what if you print it out and have someone go through it with a calculator? Does the calculator blow up? What if you only work out part of it? What if you use mental maths to solve it and no computer? It would be interesting to know if that works (doesn't need to give results, it could just be a statement that it's non-hazardous but impractical considering its transmission rate) or if it hits you a cognitohazard when you so much as think about it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: EMP would be difficult, since an EMP usually requires a nuclear weapon. There are, however, ways. A ground-based mass driver could theoretically accelerate a tungsten-steel dart up to escape velocity and kill the thing. Since it would be an unguided, nonelectronic metal slug, it wouldn't be affected by the interference it puts out. An exoatmospheric kill vehicle could be tested as well, but since they are electronically guided, it'd probably freak out and go off course, as would the ASM-131 antisatellite missile. Hell, if it came to it, we could probably accelerate an old comsat (one of the Iridium ones, perhaps. Or one of the old GAMBIT spy satellites.) to an intercept vector using all its fuel.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Did you…if that's not a load of technobabble I'll eat my hat. 2000 gigawatts is far, far beyond anything we can make today, or in the foreseeable future. The HELLADS (High Energy Liquid Laser Area Defence System) device is designed to kill incoming artillery, and it runs on 150 kilowatts. The YAL-1 system, mounted on a modified Boeing 747 is the only megawatt-class reference I could find, and it's massive and not viable. For comparison, the United States draws (if I calculated this correctly) 442582Mw per year. A 2000-Mw laser is not only overkill for a satellite (we've got satellite kill weapons, the American ASM-135, modifications to the RIM-161 SM3, and other models, notably from China and Russia), but almost impossible without immense amounts of fuel and possibly a small nuclear reactor.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Wow, 46 posts in the discussion in the first ten hours of it being posted. I doubt that's a record, but it is certainly a lot.

Anyway, to address some of the issues brought up (in no particular order):

Though I find the idea of it being in the asteroid belt or around Jupiter intriguing, I find that takes away from some of the creepiness. I also have to ask myself how in the world (puntastic!) we would have ever discovered it.

I understand some people's issue that this SCP appears somewhat "uncontained." However, to explain my logic, this SCP is being contained by observing it, which the Foundation is doing. It currently isn't doing much besides transmitting, which the Foundation is working on stopping. The Foundation does have the option of attempting to destroy it (I originally included a blurb about using a rail gun, but decided it was out of place), but destroying it may in fact cause more trouble than leaving it alone. Read up like 6 posts; Sorts has a good explanation as to why destroying it would be a bad idea.

As far as blocking or changing the data it gathers, I also considered this, but I feel as though that requires a better understanding of the SCP than is appropriate to maintain creepiness.

EDIT: Haha, I almost forgot to answer the question directly above this post. Anyway, as to space junk, I do have a plan for that, but it ties in with the [DATA EXPUNGED] in the test log, so I won't go into detail.

I hope this clears up some issues, or at least explains my logic behind them. Thanks for all the feedback guys, I really appreciate it!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Right. I like this one. Few possible solutions to Bright's issues.

1) Move it. Put it somewhere away from Earth, but still collecting data. After all, who's to say that alien technology requires that kind of proximity? I like Jovian orbit, myself. It's out of easy reach. It also makes the thing more out there, since our technology couldn't detect the things it's picking up from that range. It also hints a bit more of the things the Foundation is capable of; how else could they even find the satellite that far away?

2) Don't have the Foundation grab it or destroy it. I can easily see the Foundation deciding to leave it where it is. Instead, they figure out how it works well enough to start feeding it false data. This shows that the Foundation is doing something about it, while leaving it where it is. Possibly hint that the Foundation is uncertain whether or not they're giving data that serves the needs of Earth or not (we say we have more nukes; does it deter them, or make them see us as a threat? We say we have fewer nukes; do they decide we're not worth bothering, or that we're weak enough to attack?).

Nail the satellite instead of observing it, and you let the watchers know we're on to them — we might not find their next spy device.

So I think it is good as is and can be justified to remain in orbit for now
